transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you lately?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, it's honestly a bit difficult to even know where to begin. I'm a physician myself, so you would think I'd have a better handle on how to articulate this, but lately, I just... I guess I’m here because I feel like I absolutely do not deserve the trust that people put in me every single day. 

It's this overwhelming, heavy feeling. Patients come into the clinic, they look at me, they trust my judgment with their health, their lives, and all I can think about is how I am completely failing them. I just keep replaying these small clinical imperfections in my head. Things that, maybe in the grand scheme of a shift, are minor—like taking a little too long to recall a specific medication interaction, or second-guessing a routine dosage, or just the way I phrased something during a consultation. But I play them over and over and over again. It’s like a film reel that just won't stop running, especially when I'm driving home or trying to close my eyes at night. 

And the worst part is, the more I replay these moments, these tiny little imperfections, the more they magnify until they feel like absolute, undeniable proof that I’m a dangerous doctor. I mean, I sit there and think, how can the medical board let me practice? How can my colleagues let me near patients when I am so clearly a risk to them? I just feel this immense, crushing guilt that I'm doing harm, and even if nobody else has said anything yet, I feel like I'm just a hazard waiting to happen, and it's exhausting carrying that around all day...
Doctor: Can you describe a bit more about these thoughts that keep replaying in your mind? Are they intrusive or unwanted, and do they feel difficult to control once they start?

Intrusive really doesn't even begin to cover it, honestly. It’s more like... it's like they completely hijack my brain. I’ll be at home, maybe trying to eat dinner or just sitting on the couch trying to decompress after a twelve-hour shift, and suddenly I’m agonizing over a specific patient interaction from three days ago. And once it starts, it’s just impossible to turn off. I get so worked up, so consumed by this sinking feeling in my chest, that I actually log into the EMR from my laptop at home. I shouldn't, but I do. 

I pull up the patient's chart, and I read through every single note, the vitals, the lab results, the nursing flowsheets. And the thing is, there is absolutely nothing there to suggest a bad outcome. The chart is perfectly fine. But... but it doesn't even matter. Even when I review the chart and there’s no evidence of anything going wrong, I just can't shake it. I keep believing, with this absolute, terrifying certainty, that some routine delay on my part, or some slightly imperfect message I gave to the charge nurse, has quietly harmed the patient. 

I just sit there staring at the screen, thinking, 'The labs look fine now, but what if my delay in ordering that fluid bolus set off a cascade that hasn't shown up yet?' I convince myself that the damage is already done, just lurking under the surface. And the dread... it's suffocating, because I just know that everyone will eventually discover it. I picture the Morbidity and Mortality conference, I picture the chief of staff pulling my files, I picture the patient's family finding out that I was the one who ruined their life because I took an extra twenty minutes to respond to a page. I try to tell myself to be rational, I tell myself I'm looking right at the proof that everything is okay, but the thoughts just spiral and spiral. I can't stop them. It’s like my logical medical training completely short-circuits, and all I'm left with is this absolute conviction that I've destroyed someone's life and the clock is just ticking until I'm found out.

When these thoughts overwhelm you, do you feel driven to perform certain behaviors or mental rituals—like checking the EMR repeatedly or mentally reviewing events—to reduce the anxiety or prevent something bad from happening?

Well, I... I wouldn't call them rituals, exactly. I mean, I know what you're asking, like OCD, right? I learned about all that in med school. But it's not like I have to flip a light switch three times or wash my hands until they bleed to stop a bad outcome. It's... it's different than that. 

I do check the EMR, yes, I mentioned that. And I guess I do it a lot. But I'm not doing it to magically prevent something bad from happening. I'm doing it because I'm trying to find the bad thing that I just *know* I already did. It's like... I'm searching for the evidence of my own incompetence before someone else finds it. I'll sit there and trace back every single step of a patient's admission. I'll look at the time stamp on the ED triage note, then the time I put in the admission orders, then the time the first dose of antibiotics was actually scanned by the nurse. And I'll just stare at those times, doing the math over and over. If there was a forty-minute gap between my order and the administration, I start agonizing over whether I should have called the floor to expedite it, whether that forty minutes allowed the sepsis to progress, whether I effectively killed the patient by not picking up the phone. 

And then, yeah, I do mentally review things. Constantly. I'll be lying in bed, staring at the ceiling, and I'll replay an entire family meeting from two weeks ago. I'll try to remember exactly what words I used when explaining a prognosis. Did I sound too optimistic? Did I give them false hope? Did I fail to adequately document that I discussed the risks of the procedure? I'll just loop that conversation in my head, trying to hear my exact tone of voice, trying to see the expressions on their faces, trying to figure out exactly how I failed them. 

But it doesn't reduce the anxiety. That's the thing. It doesn't make me feel better. It actually makes it worse, because the more I look at the chart, the more I replay the conversations, the more convinced I become that I missed something crucial. I just end up finding new things to doubt, new ways I could have caused harm. So, no, it's not a ritual to relieve anxiety. It's just... it's just me trying to prepare for the inevitable fallout of my own terrible medical care, even though, deep down, I know the chart says the patient went home stable. It just doesn't matter what the chart says. I still feel like a fraud who's hurting people.
Over the past two weeks, have you experienced little interest or pleasure in doing things, or felt down, depressed, or hopeless nearly every day?

Yeah... yeah, I have. It's actually been going on for a lot longer than two weeks, to be honest. For months now, really. I just... I feel completely hollowed out. Down, hopeless, all of it. It’s like all the color has just been drained out of my life outside the hospital. 

I used to be the guy who organized everything. I would plan these really involved weekend hikes for my friends and me. I’d spend my evenings mapping out the trails, checking the elevation gains, figuring out the best routes to take... and I’d always drag myself out of bed at some ungodly hour, like 3 or 4 in the morning, just so I could get up to the summit or the ridge in time to take sunrise photos. I had all the lenses, the heavy tripod, I was just so obsessed with catching that perfect morning light breaking over the trees. It used to give me so much energy, you know? It was my reset button. 

And if I wasn't hiking, I was cooking. I used to throw these massive Indonesian dinners for my friends. I'd spend the entire weekend prepping—making beef rendang from scratch, simmering the coconut milk for hours and hours until the oil separated, grinding my own spices for the sambal, making sure there were five different side dishes and enough food for a dozen people. I loved the chaos of it, the planning, the hosting, having a house full of people laughing and eating. 

But now? For months now, I haven't done a single one of those things. My camera bag is just sitting in the corner of my bedroom gathering dust, and the idea of even going to the grocery store, let alone cooking a massive meal, just feels completely overwhelming. My friends will text me, asking when the next dinner is, or if I want to hit a trail this weekend, and I just... I stare at the phone. I make up some excuse about being post-call or having to catch up on charts. Because even the thought of doing those things... it just feels like this crushing, impossible obligation. I can't make myself care about any of it anymore. I just sit on the couch on my days off and feel this heavy, sinking hopelessness, like I don't even know who I am if I'm not functioning at work. I just have absolutely zero interest or pleasure left for the things that used to make me feel alive.
Do these thoughts or the need to check things ever take up so much time that you struggle to get through your day, or do they interfere with your ability to function at work or at home?

Well, it's... I mean, I am still showing up to clinic. I haven't missed a shift or called out sick or anything like that. I get up, I put on my badge, and I physically walk through the doors of the hospital every morning. But getting through the actual day... it's like wading through wet cement right now. 

Because my mind is so preoccupied with reviewing the charts and second-guessing every single decision I made the day before, it just drains everything out of me. It takes up so much mental space that I’ve actually had to start asking for help with all the non-urgent administrative work. Like, the in-basket messages, the routine refill requests, the prior authorizations... I used to just knock those out between patients or during my lunch break, no problem. I prided myself on having an empty inbox by 5 PM. But now? I just sit there staring at the screen, paralyzed, because I don't trust my own judgment anymore. I have to ask my MA or the covering nurses to handle the initial triage of those messages, or I'll ask one of the other attendings to look over a simple discharge summary for me, just because I... I just can't muster the mental bandwidth or the confidence to do it myself. It's embarrassing, honestly. It's definitely starting to affect how reliably I function at work, because the paperwork is piling up and people are starting to notice that I'm just not as sharp or as efficient as I used to be.

And then at home... well, I kind of mentioned this already with the dinners and the hiking, but it's not just that I'm not doing my hobbies. I actively avoid all social plans now. My buddy Dave texted me on Thursday about grabbing a beer, just a low-key thing at a place down the street, and I literally drafted like four different text messages trying to explain why I couldn't go before just telling him I was catching up on dictations, which was a lie. I avoid these things because I just... I don't have the energy, first of all. I'm so exhausted from constantly battling my own brain all day. But it's also because I just don't trust myself around people right now. I don't trust my judgment, I don't trust that I won't just sit there at the table staring blankly at the wall, completely detached from the conversation because I'm internally panicking about a patient's potassium level from three days ago. I feel like a liability to be around. So I just stay home and check the EMR. It's really affecting how connected I am outside of the hospital... I mean, I'm basically not connected to anyone at all anymore.
Do these thoughts ever feel like they are outside of your control, and do they cause significant distress even though you recognize they might be excessive or unrealistic?

Outside of my control? Yeah... I mean, absolutely. It's like... it's like a runaway train in my head, just barreling down the tracks, and I'm sitting in the conductor's seat but the brakes are completely gone. I can't stop the thoughts once they start. 

And as for whether I recognize that they're excessive or unrealistic... see, that's the part that is really, truly tearing me apart right now. Because logically, the medical training part of my brain, the part that spent years learning how to interpret data, it knows how to read a chart, right? I can look at the EMR. I can see the discharge summary. But... and this is the thing that just completely consumes me, no matter what I do... even when I review the chart, like, line by line, and there is absolutely zero evidence of a bad outcome—the vitals were perfectly stable, the labs normalized, the patient walked out the front doors of the hospital completely fine—I still can't shake it. 

I just keep believing, with this terrifying, absolute certainty, that some routine delay or some imperfect message from me has quietly harmed a patient. I'll get stuck on the idea that a pharmacy verification taking twenty minutes longer than usual, or a slightly rushed sign-out message I gave to the night float, set off this invisible chain reaction. I'll sit there sweating, thinking that there's this hidden, ticking time bomb of damage that I caused, and the chart just hasn't caught up to it yet. 

It causes so much distress because I'm just sitting around all day, waiting for the other shoe to drop. I'm just waiting for the phone call from risk management, or the email from the department chair calling me into an M&M conference. I just *know* that everyone will eventually discover it. I know they're going to pull the audit logs and see that I was negligent, that I'm the reason someone is secretly suffering out there, even if the system says they're perfectly healthy. It doesn't matter what the objective data says, or how many times I tell myself I'm being irrational. The feeling that I've ruined someone's life and I'm a fraud who is about to be exposed... it just doesn't go away. It’s always there, just gnawing at the back of my skull, no matter how many times I refresh the screen or try to talk myself down.
Have you been feeling down or hopeless even when you're not thinking about these medical concerns or reviewing patient charts?

Yeah... yeah, it’s just this constant, heavy blanket over everything. Even if I manage to force myself away from the computer, even if I'm just sitting in my living room trying to stare at the TV or something, that sinking, hollow feeling is still right there. It’s my baseline now. 

It’s... well, it’s strange, because I don't think I've mentioned this part yet, but this whole downward spiral, this entire depressive period... it actually started right after I got this clinic award. Which probably sounds completely backwards, I know. You’d think getting an award would be a good thing, right? It was this 'Physician of the Quarter' recognition, and they gave me a plaque, there was a little gathering in the breakroom... but instead of feeling proud, it just triggered this massive, crushing sense of guilt. Like I was a complete fraud. And that just morphed into this deep, dark hole that I haven't been able to climb out of since. 

And the thing is, before this... before this specific depressive period started after that award, I had never experienced anything like what's happening to my mind right now. I mean, I’d get stressed, sure, medical training is stressful, but I had never, ever heard patient voices in my head, you know? Or been so absolutely convinced that I had secretly harmed people despite all the objective evidence in the chart telling me otherwise. That is all entirely new. 

These voices, and these fixed, unshakable guilty beliefs that I'm a danger to my patients... they only show up now, when I’m in this incredibly low, guilty state. It’s like the depression opened up some kind of trapdoor in my brain. Because when I was feeling normal, before the award and this whole crash, I trusted my clinical judgment. I didn't hear things. I didn't think I was a monster hiding behind a white coat. It’s strictly tied to this... this heavy, hopeless feeling that just won't leave me alone, whether I'm actively looking at a chart or just trying to exist in my own house.
Have you ever had a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or were more impulsive than usual, to the point that others might have noticed a change in your behavior?

Well, no... I mean, not at all. Unusually energetic? No. I mean, if you look at my career path, going through medical school and residency, my sleep schedule has obviously been completely chaotic for the better part of the last decade. There were months during my intern year where I was pulling 28-hour call shifts every fourth night, so I definitely wasn't getting much sleep then. But that was never because I didn't *need* sleep, you know? It was because the hospital demanded it. I was absolutely exhausted. I would come home and just collapse into bed. I've never had a time where I woke up after two hours of sleep and felt like I could run a marathon or take on the world. Honestly, I was practically living off of bad cafeteria coffee just to keep my eyes open during morning rounds. 

And as far as being impulsive... I’ve actually always been the exact opposite of that. I've always been extremely methodical, maybe even to a fault. I'm the kind of person who plans out my meals for the week on Sunday afternoons, and I map out my clinic schedule days in advance. I don't make snap decisions. I don't go on wild spending sprees or suddenly decide to take a trip or anything like that. My friends in med school used to joke that I was the most predictable guy in our entire cohort. 

So, no, nobody has ever had to pull me aside because I was acting hyper or reckless or out of character in that way. If anything, my colleagues are only noticing a change in my behavior right now because I’m so completely drained and paralyzed by all this guilt and checking the charts. But never the other way around. I've never had a period where I felt on top of the world or anything even close to that. Just the idea of having excess energy right now sounds completely alien to me. Even on my best days, before this whole nightmare started, I was just... normal. Just a regular, somewhat tired doctor. So, no, definitely nothing like what you're describing.
Have you ever felt like you're hearing voices or believing things that others don’t, even if you’re the only one who feels that way?

Yeah... um, yes. That’s... that’s actually the part that really terrifies me the most, if I'm being completely honest. Because, you know, as a doctor, you read about these things in textbooks, but experiencing it... it's entirely different. 

It usually happens when I’m completely alone. Like, after a long day at the clinic, when I finally get home and the house is just... dead quiet, you know? Or later, when I'm lying in bed, just staring at the ceiling, trying to force myself to fall asleep, which is a whole exhausting process in itself. The ambient noise drops, the neighborhood is quiet, and my brain is still spinning from the day, and then... out of nowhere... I hear it. I hear a patient’s voice. 

And I want to be really clear here, it’s not like a passing thought, or an inner monologue, or me just remembering a stressful conversation from earlier in the day. It is an actual sound. It’s as clear as if they were standing right there in the room with me, maybe just a few feet away at the foot of the bed. And the voice just says, "You missed it." Just those three words. "You missed it." 

And it sounds so incredibly real, so physical, that my heart just drops straight into my stomach. I’ll actually sit bolt upright in bed, or if I'm out in the living room, I'll jump up and physically go check the hallway. I'll look around the corner, or I'll grab my phone and frantically check my messages, thinking maybe I left a voicethread playing on speaker, or maybe the answering service just called and someone was speaking through the device. I'll check my call logs, my texts, everything. But the screen is always dark. There’s no one in the hallway. The house is completely empty. And I just stand there in the silence, holding my phone, realizing that nothing is there. But it’s so vivid... I can't even begin to describe how deeply unsettling it is to hear someone speak directly to you, condemning you, in a completely empty room.

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, I have. It's actually been going on for a lot longer than two weeks, to be honest. For months now, really. I just... I feel completely hollowed out. Down, hopeless, all of it. It’s like all the color has just been drained out of my life outside the hospital. 

I used to be the guy who organized everything. I would plan these really involved weekend hikes for my friends and me. I’d spend my evenings mapping out the trails, checking the elevation gains, figuring out the best routes to take... and I’d always drag myself out of bed at some ungodly hour, like 3 or 4 in the morning, just so I could get up to the summit or the ridge in time to take sunrise photos. I had all the lenses, the heavy tripod, I was just so obsessed with catching that perfect morning light breaking over the trees. It used to give me so much energy, you know? It was my reset button. 

And if I wasn't hiking, I was cooking. I used to throw these massive Indonesian dinners for my friends. I'd spend the entire weekend prepping—making beef rendang from scratch, simmering the coconut milk for hours and hours until the oil separated, grinding my own spices for the sambal, making sure there were five different side dishes and enough food for a dozen people. I loved the chaos of it, the planning, the hosting, having a house full of people laughing and eating. 

But now? For months now, I haven't done a single one of those things. My camera bag is just sitting in the corner of my bedroom gathering dust, and the idea of even going to the grocery store, let alone cooking a massive meal, just feels completely overwhelming. My friends will text me, asking when the next dinner is, or if I want to hit a trail this weekend, and I just... I stare at the phone. I make up some excuse about being post-call or having to catch up on charts. Because even the thought of doing those things... it just feels like this crushing, impossible obligation. I can't make myself care about any of it anymore. I just sit on the couch on my days off and feel this heavy, sinking hopelessness, like I don't even know who I am if I'm not functioning at work. I just have absolutely zero interest or pleasure left for the things that used to make me feel alive.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions or compulsions that are time-consuming or cause significant distress or impairment in functioning, to differentiate between OCD (F42.9) and other candidates like MDD (F32.9), GAD (F41.1), or Dysthymia (F33.9).
doctor.question: Do these thoughts or the need to check things ever take up so much time that you struggle to get through your day, or do they interfere with your ability to function at work or at home?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up to clinic, but I’ve had to ask for help with non-urgent administrative work and I avoid social plans because I don’t trust my judgment or energy. It has started to affect how reliably I function at work and how connected I am outside of it.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks about how the symptoms (thoughts and checking behaviors) interfere with my ability to function at work or at home, which corresponds to the functional impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Well, it's... I mean, I am still showing up to clinic. I haven't missed a shift or called out sick or anything like that. I get up, I put on my badge, and I physically walk through the doors of the hospital every morning. But getting through the actual day... it's like wading through wet cement right now. 

Because my mind is so preoccupied with reviewing the charts and second-guessing every single decision I made the day before, it just drains everything out of me. It takes up so much mental space that I’ve actually had to start asking for help with all the non-urgent administrative work. Like, the in-basket messages, the routine refill requests, the prior authorizations... I used to just knock those out between patients or during my lunch break, no problem. I prided myself on having an empty inbox by 5 PM. But now? I just sit there staring at the screen, paralyzed, because I don't trust my own judgment anymore. I have to ask my MA or the covering nurses to handle the initial triage of those messages, or I'll ask one of the other attendings to look over a simple discharge summary for me, just because I... I just can't muster the mental bandwidth or the confidence to do it myself. It's embarrassing, honestly. It's definitely starting to affect how reliably I function at work, because the paperwork is piling up and people are starting to notice that I'm just not as sharp or as efficient as I used to be.

And then at home... well, I kind of mentioned this already with the dinners and the hiking, but it's not just that I'm not doing my hobbies. I actively avoid all social plans now. My buddy Dave texted me on Thursday about grabbing a beer, just a low-key thing at a place down the street, and I literally drafted like four different text messages trying to explain why I couldn't go before just telling him I was catching up on dictations, which was a lie. I avoid these things because I just... I don't have the energy, first of all. I'm so exhausted from constantly battling my own brain all day. But it's also because I just don't trust myself around people right now. I don't trust my judgment, I don't trust that I won't just sit there at the table staring blankly at the wall, completely detached from the conversation because I'm internally panicking about a patient's potassium level from three days ago. I feel like a liability to be around. So I just stay home and check the EMR. It's really affecting how connected I am outside of the hospital... I mean, I'm basically not connected to anyone at all anymore.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences obsessions or compulsions that are characteristic of OCD (F42.9) or if the thoughts are more in line with ruminations related to depression (F32.9/F33.9) or anxiety (F41.1).
doctor.question: Do these thoughts ever feel like they are outside of your control, and do they cause significant distress even though you recognize they might be excessive or unrealistic?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: Even when I review the chart and there’s no evidence of a bad outcome, I keep believing that some routine delay or imperfect message from me has quietly harmed a patient and that everyone will eventually discover it.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the patient's insight into their distressing thoughts (whether they recognize them as excessive or unrealistic). This directly probes whether the thoughts are obsessions or delusions. S019 addresses this by describing the beliefs as fixed and unyielding even in the face of contradictory evidence, indicating a lack of insight characteristic of delusions.

patient.answer:
Outside of my control? Yeah... I mean, absolutely. It's like... it's like a runaway train in my head, just barreling down the tracks, and I'm sitting in the conductor's seat but the brakes are completely gone. I can't stop the thoughts once they start. 

And as for whether I recognize that they're excessive or unrealistic... see, that's the part that is really, truly tearing me apart right now. Because logically, the medical training part of my brain, the part that spent years learning how to interpret data, it knows how to read a chart, right? I can look at the EMR. I can see the discharge summary. But... and this is the thing that just completely consumes me, no matter what I do... even when I review the chart, like, line by line, and there is absolutely zero evidence of a bad outcome—the vitals were perfectly stable, the labs normalized, the patient walked out the front doors of the hospital completely fine—I still can't shake it. 

I just keep believing, with this terrifying, absolute certainty, that some routine delay or some imperfect message from me has quietly harmed a patient. I'll get stuck on the idea that a pharmacy verification taking twenty minutes longer than usual, or a slightly rushed sign-out message I gave to the night float, set off this invisible chain reaction. I'll sit there sweating, thinking that there's this hidden, ticking time bomb of damage that I caused, and the chart just hasn't caught up to it yet. 

It causes so much distress because I'm just sitting around all day, waiting for the other shoe to drop. I'm just waiting for the phone call from risk management, or the email from the department chair calling me into an M&M conference. I just *know* that everyone will eventually discover it. I know they're going to pull the audit logs and see that I was negligent, that I'm the reason someone is secretly suffering out there, even if the system says they're perfectly healthy. It doesn't matter what the objective data says, or how many times I tell myself I'm being irrational. The feeling that I've ruined someone's life and I'm a fraud who is about to be exposed... it just doesn't go away. It’s always there, just gnawing at the back of my skull, no matter how many times I refresh the screen or try to talk myself down.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences persistent depressive symptoms beyond the context of their intrusive thoughts, which would support a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9 or F33.9) over other candidates like OCD (F42.9) or Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1).
doctor.question: Have you been feeling down or hopeless even when you're not thinking about these medical concerns or reviewing patient charts?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Before this depressive period after the clinic award, I had never heard patient voices or been convinced I had secretly harmed people despite evidence. The voices and fixed guilty beliefs only show up when I’m in this low, guilty state.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the depressed mood exists independently of the delusional thoughts about medical errors, which addresses the temporal relationship between the mood episode and psychotic features (i.e., that the psychotic features only occur during the depressive episode).

patient.answer:
Yeah... yeah, it’s just this constant, heavy blanket over everything. Even if I manage to force myself away from the computer, even if I'm just sitting in my living room trying to stare at the TV or something, that sinking, hollow feeling is still right there. It’s my baseline now. 

It’s... well, it’s strange, because I don't think I've mentioned this part yet, but this whole downward spiral, this entire depressive period... it actually started right after I got this clinic award. Which probably sounds completely backwards, I know. You’d think getting an award would be a good thing, right? It was this 'Physician of the Quarter' recognition, and they gave me a plaque, there was a little gathering in the breakroom... but instead of feeling proud, it just triggered this massive, crushing sense of guilt. Like I was a complete fraud. And that just morphed into this deep, dark hole that I haven't been able to climb out of since. 

And the thing is, before this... before this specific depressive period started after that award, I had never experienced anything like what's happening to my mind right now. I mean, I’d get stressed, sure, medical training is stressful, but I had never, ever heard patient voices in my head, you know? Or been so absolutely convinced that I had secretly harmed people despite all the objective evidence in the chart telling me otherwise. That is all entirely new. 

These voices, and these fixed, unshakable guilty beliefs that I'm a danger to my patients... they only show up now, when I’m in this incredibly low, guilty state. It’s like the depression opened up some kind of trapdoor in my brain. Because when I was feeling normal, before the award and this whole crash, I trusted my clinical judgment. I didn't hear things. I didn't think I was a monster hiding behind a white coat. It’s strictly tied to this... this heavy, hopeless feeling that just won't leave me alone, whether I'm actively looking at a chart or just trying to exist in my own house.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a manic or hypomanic episode, which would help differentiate between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder) and F33.9 (Recurrent Depressive Disorder) versus bipolar spectrum disorders (not current candidates but important to rule out).
doctor.question: Have you ever had a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, needed less sleep, or were more impulsive than usual, to the point that others might have noticed a change in your behavior?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of mania or hypomania (unusual energy, decreased need for sleep, impulsivity), which are not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, no... I mean, not at all. Unusually energetic? No. I mean, if you look at my career path, going through medical school and residency, my sleep schedule has obviously been completely chaotic for the better part of the last decade. There were months during my intern year where I was pulling 28-hour call shifts every fourth night, so I definitely wasn't getting much sleep then. But that was never because I didn't *need* sleep, you know? It was because the hospital demanded it. I was absolutely exhausted. I would come home and just collapse into bed. I've never had a time where I woke up after two hours of sleep and felt like I could run a marathon or take on the world. Honestly, I was practically living off of bad cafeteria coffee just to keep my eyes open during morning rounds. 

And as far as being impulsive... I’ve actually always been the exact opposite of that. I've always been extremely methodical, maybe even to a fault. I'm the kind of person who plans out my meals for the week on Sunday afternoons, and I map out my clinic schedule days in advance. I don't make snap decisions. I don't go on wild spending sprees or suddenly decide to take a trip or anything like that. My friends in med school used to joke that I was the most predictable guy in our entire cohort. 

So, no, nobody has ever had to pull me aside because I was acting hyper or reckless or out of character in that way. If anything, my colleagues are only noticing a change in my behavior right now because I’m so completely drained and paralyzed by all this guilt and checking the charts. But never the other way around. I've never had a period where I felt on top of the world or anything even close to that. Just the idea of having excess energy right now sounds completely alien to me. Even on my best days, before this whole nightmare started, I was just... normal. Just a regular, somewhat tired doctor. So, no, definitely nothing like what you're describing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences delusions or hallucinations, which would be more indicative of a psychotic disorder (e.g., F22.0, but not among current candidates) versus mood or anxiety disorders, and to help differentiate between major depressive disorder with anxious distress and obsessive-compulsive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you ever felt like you're hearing voices or believing things that others don’t, even if you’re the only one who feels that way?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: When I’m alone after clinic or trying to fall asleep, I sometimes hear a patient’s voice as clearly as if they were in the room saying, 'You missed it,' and I’ll check the hallway or my phone even though nothing is there.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hearing voices, which directly corresponds to hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Yeah... um, yes. That’s... that’s actually the part that really terrifies me the most, if I'm being completely honest. Because, you know, as a doctor, you read about these things in textbooks, but experiencing it... it's entirely different. 

It usually happens when I’m completely alone. Like, after a long day at the clinic, when I finally get home and the house is just... dead quiet, you know? Or later, when I'm lying in bed, just staring at the ceiling, trying to force myself to fall asleep, which is a whole exhausting process in itself. The ambient noise drops, the neighborhood is quiet, and my brain is still spinning from the day, and then... out of nowhere... I hear it. I hear a patient’s voice. 

And I want to be really clear here, it’s not like a passing thought, or an inner monologue, or me just remembering a stressful conversation from earlier in the day. It is an actual sound. It’s as clear as if they were standing right there in the room with me, maybe just a few feet away at the foot of the bed. And the voice just says, "You missed it." Just those three words. "You missed it." 

And it sounds so incredibly real, so physical, that my heart just drops straight into my stomach. I’ll actually sit bolt upright in bed, or if I'm out in the living room, I'll jump up and physically go check the hallway. I'll look around the corner, or I'll grab my phone and frantically check my messages, thinking maybe I left a voicethread playing on speaker, or maybe the answering service just called and someone was speaking through the device. I'll check my call logs, my texts, everything. But the screen is always dark. There’s no one in the hallway. The house is completely empty. And I just stand there in the silence, holding my phone, realizing that nothing is there. But it’s so vivid... I can't even begin to describe how deeply unsettling it is to hear someone speak directly to you, condemning you, in a completely empty room.

inference.note: The emergence of clear auditory hallucinations (e.g., hearing a patient's voice say 'You missed it' in the absence of external stimuli) that are consistent with brief psychotic disorder with delusional or hallucinatory features. The content of the hallucinations is congruent with the patient's underlying guilt and fears related to medical practice, which could also support a major depressive episode with psychotic features (F32.3 or F33.3). However, since the psychotic symptoms appear to be recent, time-limited, and closely linked to a severe depressive episode, F23.80 (Other specified psychotic disorders) or F23.3 (Brief psychotic disorder with mood symptoms) are more appropriate at this time. F32.9 and F33.9 are ruled out due to the presence of clear psychotic features. F42.9 and F41.1 are ruled out due to the presence of hallucinations and delusional thinking that go beyond OCD or anxiety.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you lately?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a constellation of symptoms consistent with an acute polymorphic psychotic disorder without symptoms of schizophrenia. The patient reports persistent, intrusive, and distressing thoughts related to perceived medical incompetence, along with auditory hallucinations (i.e., hearing a patient's voice say 'You missed it'), and a marked sense of guilt and worthlessness. These symptoms are not better explained by a major depressive episode with psychotic features or other schizophrenia-spectrum disorders, given the polymorphic nature of the psychotic features and the strong temporal association with a depressive episode.
